Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Patel (Redwood SE), Ravi Anand (Questonix CTO), Sofia Morales (Questonix Lead ML Eng), Tom Brenner (Infra), Lena Park (PM)

Redwood AE/SE outlined integration options, SDK patterns, example LangChain adapter, KV cache behavior, and fallback routing. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot: hosted eval with dedicated burst or private on-prem POC depending on PKI/tenant requirements.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private decision factors
Gateway / proxy placement and sidecar vs edge
Rate limits, quota model, token accounting
Observability hooks, traces, token-level billing, evals
transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we've got about an hour, we'll try to keep it tight. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, with Jordan our SE.
[00:00:10] Jordan: hi all, uh quick mic check, yeah all good.
[00:00:18] Ravi: good morning, thanks. we're excited to talk through how we can route our LlamaIndex workloads.
[00:00:25] Sofia: yep, Sofia here — main thing for us is PII in docs, so private or VPC is a hard requirement if hosted can't meet our compliance.
[00:00:33] Maya: totally understood. first can you share a bit of context — production traffic, average seq lengths, and who's calling the API today?
[00:00:42] Tom: sure — right now we have a batch ingestion pipeline and a user-facing Q&A service. QPS is lowish — 10 to 50 rps peak for now — but we do a lot of long contexts, average tokens per request around 1.8k to 2.5k depending on retrieval.
[00:00:58] Lena: timeline is Sort of EOY decision, wanted to evaluate hosted first then dedicated commit if costs are good.
[00:01:05] Jordan: OK that helps. long context, moderate QPS — latency SLOs?
[00:01:10] Ravi: 95th percentile under 400ms for short queries, for retrieval-augmented it's fine to be 800-1k ms, but cost per 1k tokens is important.
[00:01:20] Jordan: makes sense. On the integration side are you using LangChain or LlamaIndex directly?
[00:01:26] Sofia: LlamaIndex primarily, with some homegrown orchestration. We also have a LangChain wrapper for a few new features.
[00:01:33] Maya: perfect. so typical patterns: we surface our SDK (node/python) into your gateway, or you run our gateway-proxy as a sidecar. For LangChain/LlamaIndex we have example adapters — sample code in the repo — that swap out the calls to the Redwood client with minimal changes.
[00:01:50] Ravi: can you show the code snippet?
[00:01:53] Jordan: yeah i'll paste in the deck link after — but verbally: replace the openai client with RedwoodClient(...), the behavior for streaming and function calling is the same. there are a few nuances around kv cache if you do long running convo state.
[00:02:06] Sofia: kv cache nuance? we've been hitting token blowup in repeated context.
[00:02:12] Jordan: so our runtime exposes an optional prefix/KV cache you can enable per-route; it stores the compressed KV layers for repeated retrieval calls so subsequent requests don't re-regen earlier layers. it's compatible with llama-cached states but some models and quantized kernels behave slightly different — occasionally names like K-V vs KV get swapped in logs so watch out.
[00:02:32] Tom: does that require us to use Redwood's runtime or can it live in our proxy?
[00:02:36] Jordan: good question — the cache is runtime-level, so you get the biggest wins if you use Redwood Dedicated or Private runtime. For hosted we expose a managed cache with per-tenant TTLs. If you run the sidecar proxy you can use local result caching for non-sensitive pieces, but for true KV cache integration you'd want the runtime.
[00:02:53] Sofia: and about the gateway — we have an existing Kong-based API gateway, thinking of adding a proxy that handles batching and token accounting. recommended pattern?
[00:03:03] Maya: customers do two things: 1) lightweight sidecar/proxy in front of the service that translates LangChain calls into Redwood SDK calls and does local rate limiting; 2) for stricter control we recommend our edge gateway deployed in the VPC which can enforce per-route quotas and do routing to hosted/dedicated/private.
[00:03:18] Ravi: per-route quotas — how granular? per-user? per-API-key?
[00:03:22] Jordan: we support token-based quotas per API key and can also map to internal user ids — you can do monthly token budgets per-project or synthetic per-session caps. The rate limiter supports burst buckets and sliding window.
[00:03:33] Tom: what's the behavior when a limit is hit — 429 vs queued?
[00:03:36] Jordan: configurable — for hosted default is reject with 429 and a Retry-After, but for Dedicated you can opt for queued bursts with a small buffer and fallback to a cheaper model variant if latency budget tight.
[00:03:48] Lena: fallback to cheaper model variant — can we control similarity thresholds? we need to avoid large quality regressions.
[00:03:53] Jordan: yes, routing policies allow you to define acceptable deltas per eval set; you can pin critical endpoints to a model version and have non-critical endpoints fall back. We also expose regression alerts in Optimize tied to your eval sets.
[00:04:07] Sofia: how do we instrument observability? we need token-level cost, traces back to our request id, and per-prompt eval metrics.
[00:04:15] Maya: Console gives token breakdown per-request and a tracing ID you can inject into the SDK. For deeper observability we provide open telemetry spans and a logging hook to send events to your OTLP collector. the LangChain adapter preserves trace headers if you pass them through.
[00:04:32] Ravi: any sample dashboard or prefab panels?
[00:04:34] Jordan: yes we ship Grafana panels for cost, latency, token distribution, and model regressions. We'll drop the dashboard link in the notes.
[00:04:40] Sofia: security — our compliance team demands SOC2 plus tenant isolation and KMS integration for keys. Hosted is riskier for us unless there's a private VPC option.
[00:04:49] Maya: we have Hosted + VPC peering option for enterprise customers: private control plane with customer VPC egress and BYO KMS. Dedicated/Private give you full isolation and HSM options. we'll share the security whitepaper.
[00:04:59] Ravi: good. also curious about data retention and ephemeral logs — we can't keep any user texts beyond 30 days and need quick purge ability.
[00:05:07] Jordan: retention policy is configurable per-tenant; for private you control logs, for hosted we offer configurable retention and immediate purge APIs for compliance events. logs are encrypted at rest.
[00:05:15] Tom: on the SDK side — we want Python internal infra to call the API but prefer minimal changes to LlamaIndex. do you have a drop-in LlamaIndex connector?
[00:05:25] Jordan: yes — the connector is two thin classes: RedwoodLLM and RedwoodStreaming. Most of the LlamaIndex code uses the same call signature. caveat: function-calling deserialization is slightly different in a small set of models so we provide parsers in the adapter.
[00:05:39] Sofia: any latency overhead from adapter?
[00:05:41] Jordan: negligible — <5ms added on average. The bigger factor is network hop if you put gateway in another region, so we recommend colocating the gateway/proxy in same AZ as your service.
[00:05:51] Ravi: about batching — we do a lot of small prompts; can Redwood auto-batch across requests from different users?
[00:05:58] Jordan: yes, continuous batching in the runtime can batch similar sequence lengths, but we respect per-request latency SLOs and won't hold requests beyond the configured batch wait. For Dedicated you can tune the batch window and maximum coalesced tokens.
[00:06:12] Tom: how do you account tokens when batching? important for our billing reconciliation.
[00:06:16] Jordan: token accounting is attributed to the original request; console shows token allocation per inbound request even if batched. There's also a reconciliation export CSV that maps batch id -> constituent requests.
[00:06:27] Lena: pricing model — hosted per-token; dedicated reserved capacity — how does bursting work?
[00:06:33] Maya: hosted is per-token with tiered discounts; Dedicated is commit-based with baseline throughput. bursts are allowed within a predefined throttle window — you can configure burst capacity for spikes; overages billed at a lower per-token rate. We'll share the pricing grid.
[00:06:47] Ravi: if we start hosted and then move to private, how seamless is model pinning and rollout?
[00:06:52] Jordan: the API and rollouts are consistent — you pin model versions and rollout policies are part of the config. When you move to Dedicated/Private we sync model artifacts; some private environments require model packaging steps but code-level integration remains the same.
[00:07:03] Sofia: internal concern — our finance team wants explicit per-route quotas so we can shut off expensive endpoints programmatically. is that supported?
[00:07:10] Jordan: yes, per-route quotas and policy rules in the console have APIs so you can switch quotas or disable a route via API call.
[00:07:16] Tom: operationally we want to limit token leakage: sometimes long histories get appended accidentally. any guardrails?
[00:07:21] Maya: we recommend short-circuit helpers in SDK and a validator that rejects prompts above a token threshold. Also you can set route-level max context length.
[00:07:31] Ravi: okay, pilot mechanics — what would a Hosted pilot look like?
[00:07:35] Maya: typically a 2-week pilot: we give you trial hosted credits, a Redwood sandbox project with VPC peering if needed, and a small SE-led benchmark run to validate latency and cost using your prompt set. If it hits the compliance block we move to Dedicated eval or Private POC.
[00:07:49] Lena: how do we handle on-prem install for private — is there an appliance?
[00:07:53] Jordan: we ship a private package: control plane in your VPC and optional runtime nodes on-prem; it requires a small install script and our infra team assists with Helm charts. It is air-gapped compatible but needs vetted model artifact transfer.
[00:08:05] Sofia: model artifacts — do we bring our own? we use a few open models and some fine-tuned checkpoints.
[00:08:10] Jordan: you can bring your own model artifacts; we have onboarding docs for model packaging and quantization recommendations. We also offer to host curated open models for you.
[00:08:18] Ravi: any gotchas with LlamaIndex + long documents and embeddings pipelines?
[00:08:22] Jordan: yes — embeddings cost can be a surprise. For retrieval-heavy workloads we recommend chunking strategy and embedding dedupe caches. Also consider offloading some embedding compute to Dedicated cheaper nodes.
[00:08:34] Tom: what about rate limiting at the gateway level vs client SDK? we want defense in depth.
[00:08:39] Maya: do both — SDK-level optimistic throttling to give quick failures and gateway-level enforcement as last line. we provide rate-limit headers so you can do backoff gracefully.
[00:08:49] Sofia: can the SDK forward our internal request-id header to Redwood so traces line up?
[00:08:52] Jordan: yes include X-Request-ID, it becomes the trace id in Console. We also support custom header mappings.
[00:08:58] Ravi: security review — we will need SOC2 docs, encryption slide, and KMS integration steps.
[00:09:03] Maya: we'll send the security pack and a one pager on KMS + BYO key flow.
[00:09:07] Lena: next steps — pricing and a short bench with our sample prompts.
[00:09:10] Maya: agreed. we'll send a hosted pricing sheet, sample benchmark plan, and a LangChain/LlamaIndex adapter example.
[00:09:18] Sofia: timeline: we'll run the pilot next week if we get the credits and a small how-to.
[00:09:22] Jordan: I'll also propose a Dedicated config for your throughput so you can see commit math.
[00:09:27] Ravi: any reference customers with similar compliance needs?
[00:09:30] Maya: yes, we can share an anonymized case study of a healthcare customer who used VPC + BYO KMS.
[00:09:36] Tom: minor note — we use Kong, so if you have an example Kong plugin that'd be ideal.
[00:09:40] Jordan: we have a sample Kong plugin and a sidecar example; will attach to notes.
[00:09:45] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[00:09:47] Maya: cool, do we want to walk through the pilot steps now and set owners?
[00:09:51] Lena: yes let's do that.
[00:09:53] Maya: Jordan, you own the bench run and plugin artifacts. I'll own pricing and the security pack. Ravi/Sofia will own quick access to prompt sets and the test service.
[00:10:02] Jordan: got it. I'll set up a small test harness that runs your prompt set across hosted and dedicated sim, capture p95 latency and cost.
[00:10:10] Sofia: quick question — will the bench include token-level reconciliations? we want per-request CSV.
[00:10:14] Jordan: yes export will include per-request token footprint.
[00:10:17] Ravi: great. any other questions?
[00:10:20] Tom: one — if we need to get to private because of audit, how long does on-prem provisioning normally take?
[00:10:24] Jordan: typical lead time is 4-6 weeks for fully air-gapped on-prem with staff assist; VPC private control plane is faster — usually 2 weeks.
[00:10:33] Lena: ok that's fine.
[00:10:35] Maya: wrap-up then — recap and next steps in the notes. thanks everyone.
[00:10:40] Ravi: thanks, talk soon.
[00:10:42] (call ends)

Note: transcription contains occasional mis-hearings (e.g., \"K-V\" vs \"KV\"), speaker label swap potential.
